extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental scientists (readers of the Royal Society / 17th-century naturalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting observational and experimental natural-history notes (field and laboratory) including procedures, environmental context, comparisons to prior accounts, and quantified measurements. Emphasis on reproducible description of methods and conditions for phenomena such as insect secretions and tree sap flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provoking ants to obtain acid juice
rubrics_metrics.description: When you put the animals into water, you must stir them to make them angry, and then they will spirt out their acid juice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit procedural instruction: agitate (stir) ants to induce the secretion; the emitted liquor can be smelled (twinges the nose like newly distilled spirit of vitriol) and used for tests. This is presented as a necessary step to obtain the acid spirit from live ants for distillation or other chemical trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of staining flowers with ant juice
rubrics_metrics.description: Bare an ant-hill with a stick, and then cast the flowers upon it, and you shall see the ants creep very thick over them. Now as they creep they let fall a drop of liquor from them, and where that falls it leaves a large red stain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, repeatable field method: disturb an ant-hill, place blue flowers on it, observe drops and resultant red stains. Bruising ants and rubbing the expressed juice against the flowers produces the same staining; applies to many blue-coloured flowers. Use this as a simple qualitative assay for the presence/effect of the secretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare with known acids and chemical controls
rubrics_metrics.description: I dropped spirit of salt and oil of sulphur on the flowers, but they did not cause them to change colour... I likewise put salt of tartar on them, and dropped thereon a little spirit of salt, which caused a sufficient fermentation, but prevailed not to change the colour of the flowers in the least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run control tests using known reagents (spirit of salt, oil of sulphur, vinegar, spirit of vitriol, salt of tartar) to compare effects with the unknown ant-juice. Negative and positive controls help determine whether the substance is analogous to known acids (vinegar, vitriol) or distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation and reagent tests to characterize the acid
rubrics_metrics.description: Ants distilled by themselves, or with water, yield a spirit like spirit of vinegar, or rather like the spirit of viride aeris. Lead put into this spirit, or fair water, with the animals themselves being alive, makes a good saccharum saturni: Iron put into the spirit, affords an astringent tincture, and by repetition a crocus martis...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distillation and classical qualitative reactions (with lead, iron, salt of tartar, repeated distillation, evaporation to crystals) to infer chemical nature. Record differing reactions (e.g., producing saccharum saturni, reviving mercury into running quicksilver) to argue similarity/difference to vegetable or mineral acids. Report what distillation yields versus other starting materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record antecedent environmental conditions for tree sap phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Sycamores never bled ... unless there preceded a sensible and visible frost; for I had no other way of recording the temper of the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document meteorological antecedents (presence of frost, wind direction, timing of freeze and thaw) when reporting tree bleeding or sap runs. Note whether specific weather events (freezing, breaking up of frost) are necessary or merely contributory, and correlate timing of wounds with weather events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record timing of wounds and experimental manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The frost did not always set a bleeding the wounds, which were made before it came, though sometimes it did; but upon its breaking up, or very much relaxing the wounds either made in that instant of time, or many months before, never failed to bleed more or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When wounding trees (or otherwise manipulating subjects), record exact dates of wounds relative to environmental changes. Note whether wounds made long before an event behave differently from fresh wounds. Include wound size, depth and method (e.g., augur, cutting out a two-inch square of bark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and quantify sap yields and their diurnal variation
rubrics_metrics.description: These trees ran above two quarts in the morning. ... They ran about three quarts, and ceased about two o'clock in the afternoon, having till then continued to run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantitative measures (pints, quarts, gallons) and note the time-of-day when sap runs begin and cease. Report repeated daily measures to capture patterns (morning peak, afternoon cessation), and include sample sizes (e.g., 24 birches) to indicate variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use meteorological instruments and compare organismal indicators with instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: My weather glasses continued at the same station all this day ... though my trees have altered their temper so much ... These 24 birches began to run presently after sun-rise ... My weather glass at noon was advanced from 9 to 10½, yet the quantity of birch water this day exceeded my former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect instrumental meteorological data (barometer/weather glass, wind observations) and compare with biological indicators (trees running). Note discrepancies and consider organismal responses (e.g., wind stalling sap) as potentially more sensitive than instruments. Record instrument readings alongside biological measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test across multiple species and record negative findings
rubrics_metrics.description: I forthwith struck the hawthorn, hazel, wild rose, gooseberry bush, apple tree, cherry tree, blather nut, apricot, cherry-laurel, vine, walnut; yet none bled but the last; and that faintly in comparison of the sycamore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating a phenomenon, trial many candidate species/subjects and report both positive and negative results. Listing species tried, and their comparative responses, strengthens claims about specificity of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select candidate insects by sensory cues (pungent odor) for chemical assays
rubrics_metrics.description: Having observed that an ant bruised and smelt to emits a strange fiery and piercing odour ... by this means I have ... found an insect which I suspect may yield an acid liquor as well as the ant; and that is the long and round bodied red coloured julus...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readily detectable cues (strong pungent smell when crushed) to identify other organisms likely to yield similar chemical secretions. Use these heuristics to prioritize specimens for collection and chemical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and test alternative hypotheses; document reasoning and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: At first I guessed that ... they might thrust their stings into the flowers, and through them convey that acid liquor: But by bruising them, and rubbing the expressed juice against the flowers, I find they will be equally stained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly propose plausible mechanisms (e.g., stinging vs. secretion) and design simple tests to distinguish them (e.g., bruising vs. allowing ants to sting). Report the experiments that support or refute each hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite prior observers and situate new observations in literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Lately consulting Langham's Garden of Health, I met with this passage ... I find it delivered by Hieronymus Tragus ... Neumann and Margraaf deserve particularly to be mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare new findings to prior reports (ancient and contemporary), cite sources (Pliny, Langham, Neumann, Margraaf), and discuss continuity or novelty. Use citations to corroborate observations or note differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize mathematical/geometrical solutions by distinct cases with figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem. ... The problem has six cases. See pl. 13, fig. 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Case I. — If the station be taken without the triangle ... Case II. — If the station be in one of the sides ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a geometric/chorographical solution, enumerate and separate distinct positional cases, refer to numbered figures/plates, and give stepwise constructive methods for each case so that a reader can reproduce the geometric construction or calculation.
